key_responsibilities: Develop and maintain embedded software for bare-metal and RTOS-based systems
Implement and test digital communication protocols (SPI, I2C, UART, CAN)
Contribute to state machines and command/control software for autonomous vehicle systems
Write reliable, memory-conscious embedded software, primarily in Rust
Integrate, debug, and validate hardware-software interfaces with hardware engineers
Develop unit and integration tests using hardware test stands

strengths: Bare-metal + RTOS depth is real, not surface: STM32 Bare-Metal Temperature Monitor programs GPIO/TIM2/ADC1/I2C1 directly in C with interrupt-driven sampling, and Object Tracking Turret runs FreeRTOS with mutexes for shared-memory task coordination.

Hardware-software integration is demonstrated end to end, not just claimed: Turret sends YOLO detections from Jetson to STM32 over UART to drive servo PWM; COFFIN capstone wires Jetson+Arduino to dual ToF sensors over an I2C mux and resolved 11 real integration failures (servo brown-out, stale frames) to hit 100% pick reliability.

Command/control software for autonomous vehicle-adjacent systems has a direct analog: the CARLA project implements an actual control stack (lane-following, waypoint fallback) validated across multiple laps with zero collisions, closer to 'command/control for autonomous vehicles' than most early-career embedded resumes.

Robotics/automotive/aerospace-hardware domain fit is a genuine standout for an early-career candidate given the breadth (STM32, Jetson, ROS2 arms, CARLA, PCB fabrication) — this is explicitly called out as a preferred qualification, not just basic.
real_gaps: Zero Rust exposure anywhere in the profile — every embedded bullet is C or C++. The JD names Rust as the primary language for this specific role ('write reliable, memory-conscious embedded software, primarily in Rust'), which is more central than a simple checkbox skill even though the basic requirement only asks for willingness to learn it.
CAN bus is completely absent — no project or internship bullet mentions CAN anywhere, unlike SPI/I2C/UART which all have real project backing.

No demonstrated formal test practice for embedded systems — every project is verified by ad hoc trial counts ('10/10 trials', 'verified in Proteus') rather than unit/integration tests against hardware test stands, which is an explicit JD responsibility.

No explicit state machine design work — FreeRTOS task/mutex coordination and UART command handling are state-machine-adjacent, but no bullet actually describes designing or implementing a state machine.

No classical control theory (PID, closed-loop control laws) despite kinematics-heavy robotics experience — the arm projects are forward/inverse kinematics and trajectory planning, not feedback control tuning, so 'control systems, PID controllers, motion control' in the preferred quals isn't really backed.
overstated_by_keywords: SPI — listed in the skills section ('UART/I2C/SPI') and counted as Have in the keyword match, but no single project or internship bullet actually describes implementing or debugging an SPI interface. I2C and UART both have concrete bullet-level backing; SPI does not.

Oscilloscopes/Logic Analyzers — listed as tools and counted toward the 'hardware debugging' match, but no bullet narrates an actual debugging session using them (e.g., diagnosing a timing issue or signal fault). The STM32 temperature monitor was 'verified in Proteus' (simulation), not bench-debugged with a scope.
State machines — classified as Adjacent in the keyword pass on the assumption that FreeRTOS/embedded work implies it, but there's no direct evidence in any bullet.
llm_analysis.reasoning: The keyword match (85%) overstates readiness because it credits SPI, oscilloscope/logic-analyzer debugging, and state machines on the strength of adjacent embedded work rather than direct bullet evidence, and it doesn't weight Rust heavily since the JD phrases it as a soft 'willingness to learn.' The real profile is strong on bare-metal/RTOS fundamentals and genuinely differentiated on autonomous-systems domain fit, but has a real, not cosmetic, gap on the one thing the JD is most specific about: writing production embedded software in Rust with formal hardware test practices, plus no CAN or PID experience at all.
